events.feedback:
Yes. This one has **excellent material**, and I think it could become one of the strongest plant records in the collection. The conservation story is genuinely remarkable, and the palm itself has some unusually good identification features.

I did check the current external evidence on the conservation and distribution claims because those are important enough that I wouldn't want to simply rubber-stamp them. Kew currently lists *Archontophoenix myolensis* as accepted, endemic to NE Queensland, and IUCN Vulnerable; Queensland and Australian sources list it as Endangered. ([Plants of the World Online][1])

Your opening quick hit is powerful:

> “Fewer than 100 mature Myola King Palms are estimated to survive in the wild…”

But **this is the first thing I'd verify/revise**.

events.summary: All changes implement the reviewer's feedback precisely: the contested 'fewer than 100' population figure is replaced with verified range and status language; conservation status is corrected to reflect Endangered under both Queensland NCA and Australian federal EPBC (not state-level only); specific threats are named; altitude is corrected to 350–400 m throughout; the wildlife section's broken paragraph and speculative inferences are repaired; the quick hits are reordered and reworded per the reviewer's explicit direction; and style, trunk diameter, and propagation wording are tightened throughout.

events.feedback:
Here is a deep-dive audit of the draft page for Myola King Palm (Archontophoenix myolensis):

Botanical & Ecological Accuracy

Conservation & Range: Outstanding narrative depth. Highlighting its narrow endemic status along the Barron River and Warrill Creek (Atherton Tableland, Queensland), its Endangered status in Australia, and its 1994 description by John Dowe gives this entry excellent conservation value.

Reproductive Biology: The explanation of proterandrous monoecy (male flowers shedding pollen before female flowers open to promote cross-pollination) is accurate and well-explained.

Morphological Cues: The leaf structure (silver-grey undersides, lack of ramenta on midribs) and fruit details (eccentric stigmatic scar) provide clear diagnostic markers that separate it from Bangalow (A. cunninghamiana) and Alexandra Palm (A. alexandrae).
events.summary: The reviewer's feedback is purely confirmatory — it praises the conservation narrative, proterandrous monoecy explanation, and morphological diagnostic markers without requesting any changes to any field. No content was altered.
